## Functions

1. Write a function to compute a confidence interval around a mean. If the sample size is less than 30, your function should use a bootstrap distribution. If the sample size is at least 30, your function should use a t-distribution. Set the default confidence level to 0.95 (your function should allow for different confidence levels, though). Your function should be appropriately commented.

```{r}
confidence_function <- function(x, conf= 0.95) {
  if(length(x) < 30) {
    for (i in length(x)){
      n <- sample(x, length(x), replace = TRUE, prob = NULL)
      x[i] <- mean(n)
    }
    quantile_bootstrap <- quantile(x, probs = seq(0.025,0.975,0.95))
    return(quantile_bootstrap)
  } 
  else {
    t.test(x)
    quantile_t <- quantile(x, probs = seq(0.025,0.975,0.95))
    return(quantile_t)
  }
}
```


2. Test your function on the following datasets, which are random samples from a standard normal distribution. Do the confidence intervals you've created make sense? Can you identify a pattern? Explain.

```{r}
data_1 <- rnorm(n=10)
data_2 <- rnorm(n=20)
data_3 <- rnorm(n=40)
data_4 <- rnorm(n=100)
```

```{r}
confidence_function(data_1)
confidence_function(data_2)
confidence_function(data_3)
confidence_function(data_4)
```
When looking at the confidence intervals, all of them do make sense. They make sense because on a normal distribution you would expect the values of the lower percentile to be less than 0 and the higher percentile to be above 0. In this case it is hard to identify a pattern that is taking place. An estimate could be as the sample size increases, the more normal the distribution becomes. this is due to the centeral limit theorem.
